claims.claim: The temporally integrating neural activity in AWB neurons occurs within the AWB neuron itself and does not require a recurrent circuit.
claims.source: In the unc-13 and unc-31 mutants, however, the AWB responses were essentially similar to that in wild-type animals and fitted with the same leaky integrator equations (Figure 6A and Table 2), indicating that the temporally integrating neural activity occurs within the AWB neuron itself and does not require a recurrent circuit.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data from unc-13 and unc-31 mutants shown in Figure 6A and Table 2, with inference from the genetic manipulation.

claims.claim: ODR-3 Gα protein plays a time-differential role in the sensory signaling of AWB neurons.
claims.source: Two alleles of loss-of-function mutations of the odr-3 gene, however, caused gradual activations of AWB neurons, whose peaks were even larger than those of wild-type animals (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, black lines), suggesting that ODR-3 may play an inhibitory role in sensory signaling. Interestingly, while the AWB response patterns in wild-type animals were fitted by a leaky integrator equation with a time interval for the input (∆t)=1 s (solid red lines in Figure 4B and dotted red line in 6B), AWB response patterns in odr-3 mutants were better fitted by an equation with ∆t longer than 1 min than by ∆t = 1 s (solid red line in Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; see also Table 2 for parameters and Table 4 for goodness of fit). Thus, the time-differential property for the sensory input was greatly degraded with the odr-3 mutations while the time-integral property was not affected.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data from odr-3 mutants and mathematical modeling shown in Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, and Tables 2 and 4.

claims.claim: An egl-19 reduction-of-function mutation significantly affected the AWB response.
claims.source: We found that an egl-19 reduction-of-function mutation (rf) (Lee et al., 1997) significantly affected the AWB response (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data from egl-19 mutants shown in Figure 7A, with citation to the mutation characterization.

claims.claim: Treatment with the EGL-19 antagonist Nemadipine-A (NemA) exhibited a similar or possibly even stronger effect on AWB response than the egl-19 reduction-of-function mutation.
claims.source: Consistently, treatment with the EGL-19 antagonist Nemadipine-A (NemA) (Kwok et al., 2006) exhibited a similar, or possibly even stronger, effect.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by pharmacological experimental data with citation to NemA.

claims.claim: Mutations in unc-2, itr-1, or unc-68 did not significantly affect the AWB response.
claims.source: In contrast, mutations in unc-2, itr-1 (the IP3R ortholog) or unc-68 (the RyR ortholog) (Dal Santo et al., 1999; Sakube et al., 1997; Schafer and Kenyon, 1995) did not significantly affect the response (Figure 7A and C left panel).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data from mutants shown in Figure 7A and C, with citations to gene characterizations.

claims.claim: The calcium accumulation in AWB neurons mostly depends on influx through the EGL-19 L-type VGCCs, but not other calcium channels.
claims.source: These results suggest that the calcium accumulation in AWB neurons mostly depends on influx through the EGL-19 L-type VGCCs, but not other calcium channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic and pharmacological experimental data on calcium channels.

claims.claim: Suppression of EGL-19 with NemA mainly affected the later phase of the ASH response, but did not significantly affect the initial response.
claims.source: In ASH neurons, whose response pattern was also not affected by synaptic connections (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), the suppression of EGL-19 with NemA mainly affected the later phase of the response, but did not significantly affect the initial response (Figure 7B and C right panel).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 7B and C.

claims.claim: The ASH response consists of both fast and slow components.
claims.source: The mathematical addition of the AWB-like time-integral response to the NemA-treated ASH response resembled the wild-type ASH response (Figure 7D), suggesting that the ASH response consists of both fast and slow components.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from mathematical modeling of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The fast component of ASH response is not mediated by typical VGCCs.
claims.source: This fast component was not affected by a loss-of-function mutation in unc-2 or in a T-type VGCC homolog, cca-1 (Steger et al., 2005), suggesting that this calcium response is not mediated by the typical VGCCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from genetic experimental data with citation to cca-1 characterization.

claims.claim: Suppressing CICR by mutations of itr-1 or unc-68, or using dantrolene, partially affected the magnitude but not the temporal pattern of the ASH response.
claims.source: Suppressing CICR by mutations of itr-1 or unc-68, or using dantorolene, a RyR antagonist (Krause et al., 2004), partially affected the magnitude, but not the temporal pattern, of the ASH response regardless of NemA treatment (Figure 7B and C right panel).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by genetic and pharmacological experimental data shown in Figure 7B and C, with citation to dantrolene.

claims.claim: The ASH response may be mediated by rapid calcium influx via an unidentified type of calcium channels and by slow influx via EGL-19 L-type VGCCs, both of which are amplified by CICR.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that the ASH response may be mediated by rapid calcium influx via an unidentified type of calcium channels and by slow influx via EGL-19 L-type VGCCs, both of which are amplified by CICR.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined genetic and pharmacological experimental data.

claims.claim: C. elegans olfactory behavior comprises discrete behavioral choice based on sensory information, where animals choose either a high-turning state (pirouette) or low-turning state (run) based on dC/dt.
claims.source: Based on the results obtained in our system, we consider that the olfactory behavior of the animals comprises two essential features of decision-making at the behavioral level. (1) Discrete behavioral choice based on sensory information: Based on dC/dt, C. elegans choose either a high-turning state (pirouette) or low-turning state (run), which were shown to be physiologically distinct (Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data on behavioral states and their physiological distinctness.

claims.claim: The time required for the transition from a high-turning state to a low-turning state is shorter when the odor concentration decreases rapidly, and is longer when the concentration decreases slowly.
claims.source: (2) Timing of decision: The time required for the transition from a high-turning state to a low-turning state is shorter when the odor concentration decreases rapidly, and is longer when the concentration decreases slowly (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The temporal integration in AWB neurons can be regarded as 'evidence accumulation' for decision-making.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that [Ca2+]i is accumulated in AWB neurons according to a leaky integrator equation of odor concentration change, which is correlated with the behavioral transition (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Because odor concentration is a critical piece of information for the choice of behavioral states, the temporal integration in AWB neurons can be regarded as the 'evidence accumulation' for decision-making.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the calcium imaging data and its correlation with behavioral transitions.

claims.claim: ASH neurons respond to unfavorable changes in odor concentration in a time-differential manner and initiate turns rapidly.
claims.source: ASH neurons respond to unfavorable changes in the odor concentration in a time-differential manner and initiate turns rapidly.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging and behavioral data.

claims.claim: AWB neurons extract long-term information about favorable changes in odor concentration using the time-integral property, which leads to 'deliberate' transitions from pirouettes to runs.
claims.source: In contrast, AWB neurons extract long-term information about favorable changes in odor concentration using the time-integral property, which leads to 'deliberate' transitions from pirouettes to runs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging and behavioral data.

claims.claim: ODR-3 Gα protein is homologous to the inhibitory Gαi proteins.
claims.source: Because ODR-3 is homologous to the inhibitory Gαi proteins (Bargmann, 2006), it is possible that the sensory signal via another unidentified Gα might be downregulated by the activity of ODR-3—such an inhibitory feed-forward loop could compute the time-differential of the input (Figure 8B, left) (Alon, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on ODR-3 and by citation to the concept of inhibitory feed-forward loops.

claims.claim: L-type VGCCs are known to be activated continuously during depolarization, unlike N/P/Q-type or T-type VGCCs.
claims.source: In agreement with this model, L-type, but not N/P/Q-type or T-type, VGCCs are known to be activated continuously during depolarization (Hille, 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established knowledge about VGCC properties.

claims.claim: Temporal integration of sensory information for behavioral choice in C. elegans during odor avoidance is analogous to evidence accumulation in perceptual decision-making in mammals.
claims.source: In principle, temporal integration of sensory information for behavioral choice in C. elegans during odor avoidance is analogous to evidence accumulation in perceptual decision-making in mammals. In both cases, animals extract a long-term trend in sensory information by temporally integrating the information for decision-making (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Schall, 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations to mammalian decision-making literature.

claims.claim: Temporally integrating neural activity in higher animals is generally considered to be mediated by recurrent neural circuits.
claims.source: In higher animals, temporally integrating neural activity is required for decision-making as well as for other brain functions, such as working memory, and is generally considered to be mediated by recurrent neural circuits (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Schall, 2001; Wang, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on neural mechanisms of decision-making and working memory.

claims.claim: Temporally integrating neural activity has been suggested to be mediated by intracellular calcium signaling within a cell, but this had not been demonstrated experimentally prior to this study.
claims.source: This temporally integrating activity has also been suggested to be mediated by intracellular calcium signaling within a cell (Curtis and Lee, 2010; Loewenstein and Sompolinsky, 2003; Major and Tank, 2004); however, this had not been demonstrated experimentally.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical work and the statement that experimental demonstration was lacking.

claims.claim: The odor avoidance behavior of C. elegans is regulated by dopamine.
claims.source: Interestingly, the odor avoidance behavior of C. elegans is regulated by dopamine (Kimura et al., 2010), a neuromodulator involved in mammalian decision-making (Schultz, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on dopamine's role in C. elegans odor avoidance and mammalian decision-making.

claims.claim: C. elegans avoids the odorant 2-nonanone.
claims.source: C. elegans avoids the odorant 2-nonanone, and this odor avoidance behavior is regulated by stimulus-dependent transitions between the two behavioral states, 'pirouette' (a period of short migrations divided by turns) and 'run' (a period of long straight migration) (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Bargmann et al., 1993; Kimura et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The pirouette strategy is a form of 'biased random walk' and is the major behavioral strategy used by C. elegans for chemotaxis and thermotaxis.
claims.source: The pirouette strategy (a form of 'biased random walk') is the major behavioral strategy used by these animals for chemotaxis and thermotaxis, and the choice of migratory direction at run initiation is considered to be random in this strategy (Lockery, 2011; Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on C. elegans navigation strategies.

claims.claim: In typical chemotaxis such as salt-taxis in C. elegans, the animal initiates runs mostly in a random direction after a pirouette.
claims.source: Typical chemotaxis such as salt-taxis in C. elegans is regulated by the pirouette (i.e., biased random walk) strategy, where the animal initiates runs mostly in a random direction after a pirouette (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Increases in neural activity during the delay period according to sensory information ('evidence accumulation') has been described as a key physiological basis for the timing of decision-making in primates and rodents.
claims.source: In primates and rodents, increases in neural activity during the delay period according to the sensory information ('evidence accumulation') has been described as a key physiological basis for the timing of decision-making (Carandini and Churchland, 2013; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Schall, 2001; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on decision-making in primates and rodents.

claims.claim: Clear sensory information causes a faster rise in neuronal firing rate to a threshold and faster behavioral choice, whereas uncertain information causes a slower rise in the firing rate and slower behavioral choice.
claims.source: For example, clear sensory information causes a faster rise in neuronal firing rate to a threshold and faster behavioral choice, whereas uncertain information causes a slower rise in the firing rate and slower behavioral choice.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about decision-making mechanisms.

claims.claim: Theoretical studies suggest that evidence accumulation is mediated by recurrent neural circuits.
claims.source: Theoretical studies suggest that evidence accumulation is mediated by recurrent neural circuits (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Wang, 2008) while intracellular mechanisms, such as calcium signaling via N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, calcium-activated nonspecific cation (CAN) channels, and/or voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs), have also been proposed (Curtis and Lee, 2010; Major and Tank, 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claims.claim: Intracellular mechanisms such as calcium signaling via NMDA receptors, CAN channels, and/or VGCCs have been proposed for evidence accumulation.
claims.source: Theoretical studies suggest that evidence accumulation is mediated by recurrent neural circuits (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Wang, 2008) while intracellular mechanisms, such as calcium signaling via N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, calcium-activated nonspecific cation (CAN) channels, and/or voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs), have also been proposed (Curtis and Lee, 2010; Major and Tank, 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical studies proposing intracellular mechanisms.

claims.claim: A neuron that biases decisions was identified based on optical monitoring of neuronal activities in the medical leech.
claims.source: For example, a neuron that biases decisions was identified based on optical monitoring of the neuronal activities in the medical leech (Briggman et al., 2005), and genetic analyses identified a neuropeptide and a catecholamine receptor that underpin simple decision-making tasks in Drosophila melanogaster and in Caenorhabditis elegans, respectively (Bendesky et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to work on the medical leech.

claims.claim: Genetic analyses identified a neuropeptide and a catecholamine receptor that underpin simple decision-making tasks in Drosophila melanogaster and in Caenorhabditis elegans, respectively.
claims.source: For example, a neuron that biases decisions was identified based on optical monitoring of the neuronal activities in the medical leech (Briggman et al., 2005), and genetic analyses identified a neuropeptide and a catecholamine receptor that underpin simple decision-making tasks in Drosophila melanogaster and in Caenorhabditis elegans, respectively (Bendesky et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to genetic studies in Drosophila and C. elegans.

claims.claim: A recent behavioral study showed that Drosophila temporally accumulates sensory evidence for decision-making.
claims.source: In addition, a recent behavioral study showed that Drosophila temporally accumulates sensory evidence for decision-making (DasGupta et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a behavioral study in Drosophila.

claims.claim: AWB neurons are primarily responsible for 2-nonanone avoidance.
claims.source: First, we investigated a pair of AWB olfactory neurons. AWB neurons are known to be primarily responsible for 2-nonanone avoidance and to exhibit an odor-OFF response when animals were stimulated with 2-nonanone-saturated buffer in a stepwise manner (Ha et al., 2010; Troemel et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on AWB neurons.

claims.claim: AWB neurons exhibit an odor-OFF response when animals are stimulated with 2-nonanone-saturated buffer in a stepwise manner.
claims.source: AWB neurons are known to be primarily responsible for 2-nonanone avoidance and to exhibit an odor-OFF response when animals were stimulated with 2-nonanone-saturated buffer in a stepwise manner (Ha et al., 2010; Troemel et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on AWB neurons.

claims.claim: ASH neurons are a pair of nociceptive neurons.
claims.source: In addition, we also found that ASH neurons, a pair of nociceptive neurons (Bargmann, 2006; Kaplan, 1996), were activated by an odor increase (Figures 3D, 60–90 s).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work characterizing ASH neurons.

claims.claim: Dynamic changes in [Ca2+]i in the cell bodies of C. elegans sensory neurons are generally similar to those in axons, which cause neurotransmitter release.
claims.source: In C. elegans' sensory neurons, dynamic changes in [Ca2+]i in the cell bodies are generally similar to those in axons, which cause neurotransmitter release from the neurons (Kato et al., 2014; Zahratka et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on calcium dynamics in C. elegans neurons.

claims.claim: Time-differential properties have been suggested for the transient responses of ASH and other sensory neurons with all-or-none stimuli in C. elegans.
claims.source: Time-differential properties have been suggested for the transient responses of ASH and other sensory neurons with all-or-none stimuli in C. elegans (Lockery, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Time-differential properties have been reported in a recent study of Drosophila olfactory neurons.
claims.source: This property has also been reported in a recent study of Drosophila olfactory neurons (Schulze et al., 2015) and is in agreement with the general idea that dynamic signal changes are mediated by phasic sensory receptors (Delcomyn, 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to work on Drosophila olfactory neurons and general sensory receptor properties.

claims.claim: Dynamic signal changes are mediated by phasic sensory receptors.
claims.source: This property has also been reported in a recent study of Drosophila olfactory neurons (Schulze et al., 2015) and is in agreement with the general idea that dynamic signal changes are mediated by phasic sensory receptors (Delcomyn, 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established knowledge about sensory receptors.

claims.claim: ASH neurons temporally integrate sensory signals over several seconds.
claims.source: This is consistent with the recent report that ASH neurons temporally integrate sensory signals over several seconds (Kato et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on ASH neurons.

claims.claim: AIZ interneurons are the major postsynaptic targets of AWB neurons.
claims.source: AIZ interneurons, the major postsynaptic targets of AWB neurons (White et al., 1986), have been shown to elicit digital-like excitability and trigger turns upon activation (Li et al., 2014), suggesting that AWB neurons inactivate AIZ neurons in an all-or-none manner at a certain threshold.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the C. elegans connectome.

claims.claim: AIZ interneurons elicit digital-like excitability and trigger turns upon activation.
claims.source: AIZ interneurons, the major postsynaptic targets of AWB neurons (White et al., 1986), have been shown to elicit digital-like excitability and trigger turns upon activation (Li et al., 2014), suggesting that AWB neurons inactivate AIZ neurons in an all-or-none manner at a certain threshold.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on AIZ interneurons.

claims.claim: ODR-3 is expressed in AWB, ASH and a few other pairs of sensory neurons.
claims.source: ODR-3, one of the 20 Gα homologs in C. elegans, is expressed in AWB, ASH and a few other pairs of sensory neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ODR-3 expression.

claims.claim: ODR-3 is localized at the sensory ending.
claims.source: It is localized at the sensory ending, and its dysfunction causes severe chemotaxis defects, suggesting that ODR-3 transduces the sensory signal from odorant receptor (Roayaie et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on ODR-3 localization.

claims.claim: Dysfunction of ODR-3 causes severe chemotaxis defects.
claims.source: It is localized at the sensory ending, and its dysfunction causes severe chemotaxis defects, suggesting that ODR-3 transduces the sensory signal from odorant receptor (Roayaie et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on ODR-3 function.

claims.claim: Previous studies have demonstrated the requirement for EGL-19 and/or UNC-2 in the responses of sensory neurons of C. elegans.
claims.source: Previous studies have demonstrated the requirement for EGL-19 and/or UNC-2, the sole orthologs of L- and N-type channels, respectively, in the responses of sensory neurons of C. elegans (Busch et al., 2012; Frøkjaer-Jensen et al., 2006; Hilliard et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2014; Larsch et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2003; Zahratka et al., 2015) although their precise roles in intracellular calcium dynamics have remained unclear.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies on calcium channels in C. elegans.

claims.claim: EGL-19 and UNC-2 are the sole orthologs of L- and N-type calcium channels, respectively, in C. elegans.
claims.source: Previous studies have demonstrated the requirement for EGL-19 and/or UNC-2, the sole orthologs of L- and N-type channels, respectively, in the responses of sensory neurons of C. elegans (Busch et al., 2012; Frøkjaer-Jensen et al., 2006; Hilliard et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2014; Larsch et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2003; Zahratka et al., 2015) although their precise roles in intracellular calcium dynamics have remained unclear.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: The precise roles of EGL-19 and UNC-2 in intracellular calcium dynamics have remained unclear prior to this study.
claims.source: Previous studies have demonstrated the requirement for EGL-19 and/or UNC-2, the sole orthologs of L- and N-type channels, respectively, in the responses of sensory neurons of C. elegans (Busch et al., 2012; Frøkjaer-Jensen et al., 2006; Hilliard et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2014; Larsch et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2003; Zahratka et al., 2015) although their precise roles in intracellular calcium dynamics have remained unclear.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations and the statement that precise roles were unclear.

claims.claim: In previous studies, ASH response was significantly suppressed by NemA-treatment as well as by the egl-19(n582) mutation upon stimulation with 1-octanol.

claims.claim: ASH response was essentially unaffected by the egl-19(n582) mutation upon stimulation with glycerol.
claims.source: In previous studies, ASH response was significantly suppressed by NemA-treatment as well as by the egl-19(n582) mutation upon stimulation with another repulsive odorant (1-octanol) (Zahratka et al., 2015) although ASH response was essentially unaffected by the same egl-19 mutation upon stimulation with glycerol (Pokala et al., 2014), suggesting that different sensory stimuli may be processed differently in the polymodal ASH neurons.

claims.claim: Different sensory stimuli may be processed differently in the polymodal ASH neurons.

claims.claim: C. elegans sensory neurons possess higher-order functions such as learning and memory because of the quite small number of neurons in their nervous system.
claims.source: While AWBs are sensory neurons, their integration property may reflect a central nervous system-like function; C. elegans' sensory neurons are known to possess higher-order functions, such as learning and memory, because of the quite small number of neurons in their nervous system (de Bono and Maricq, 2005; Sasakura and Mori, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on C. elegans sensory neuron functions.

claims.claim: The resting calcium concentration in neurons is generally about 100 nM.
claims.source: The estimated calcium concentration exhibited a similar pattern to the measured fluorescence change with an estimated basal concentration of about 60–90 nM (Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Table 2), similar to that generally reported for resting neurons in general (~100 nM) (Clapham, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established knowledge about neuronal calcium concentrations.

claims.claim: The calcium affinity (Kd) of GCaMP3 is 405 nM.
claims.source: The calcium affinity (Kd = 405 nM) used for the estimation was according to Akerboom et al. (2012).

claims.claim: The dynamic range (Fmax/Fmin) of GCaMP3 is about 12-fold.
claims.source: For GCaMP3, fmax=12fmin since the dynamic range Fmax/Fmin (i.e., fmax/fmin) is reported to be ~12 fold (Tian et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the GCaMP3 characterization study.

claims.claim: The association and dissociation time constants of GCaMP3 are of the sub-second order.
claims.source: The time delay of fluorescence response to a calcium concentration change was not taken into account since the temporal resolution of the odor concentration measurement was of the second order, while the association and dissociation time constants of GCaMP3 are of the sub-second order (Tian et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the GCaMP3 characterization study.

claims.claim: UNC-13 is the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian Munc-13.
claims.source: To determine whether a synaptic circuit input is required for the temporally integrating property of AWB neurons, we abolished the transmission of synaptic and/or dense core vesicles in most, if not all, neurons via a mutation in unc-13 or unc-31, the orthologs of mammalian Munc-13 and CAPS (calcium activated protein for secretion), respectively (Richmond, 2005).

claims.claim: UNC-31 is the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian CAPS (calcium activated protein for secretion).

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on UNC-31.

claims.claim: The signaling pathway mediating odor response in AWB neurons is similar to that in mammalian olfactory/photoreceptor neurons.
claims.source: Previous genetic studies suggest that the signaling pathway mediating odor response in AWB neurons is similar to that in mammalian olfactory/photoreceptor neurons. Upon binding to an odorant, a G-protein coupled receptor activates Gα protein, which eventually leads to the opening of cyclic nucleotide-gated cation channels for depolarization (Bargmann, 2006).

claims.claim: Upon binding to an odorant, a G-protein coupled receptor activates Gα protein, which eventually leads to the opening of cyclic nucleotide-gated cation channels for depolarization in AWB neurons.
claims.source: Upon binding to an odorant, a G-protein coupled receptor activates Gα protein, which eventually leads to the opening of cyclic nucleotide-gated cation channels for depolarization (Bargmann, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established knowledge about AWB signaling.

claims.claim: C. elegans has 20 Gα homologs.

claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about C. elegans genetics.

claims.claim: Increases in [Ca2+]i in neurons can occur via influx through the plasma membrane via VGCCs and can trigger rapid calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum via IP3Rs and/or RyRs as calcium-induced calcium release (CICR).

claims.claim: UNC-68 is the C. elegans ortholog of ryanodine receptor.

claims.claim: Dantrolene is a RyR antagonist.
claims.source: Suppressing CICR by mutations of itr-1 or unc-68, or using dantorolene, a RyR antagonist (Krause et al., 2004), partially affected the magnitude, but not the temporal pattern, of the ASH response regardless of NemA treatment (Figure 7B and C right panel).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on dantrolene.

claims.claim: CCA-1 is a T-type VGCC homolog in C. elegans.
claims.source: This fast component was not affected by a loss-of-function mutation in unc-2 or in a T-type VGCC homolog, cca-1 (Steger et al., 2005), suggesting that this calcium response is not mediated by the typical VGCCs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on CCA-1.

claims.claim: Brains regulate behavioral responses with distinct timings ranging from milliseconds to days.
claims.source: Brains process sensory information to generate various kinds of physiological responses with different timings (i.e., with different latencies to respond): For example, motor control, foraging, decision-making and the sleep-wake cycle range on timescales from milliseconds to days (Buhusi and Meck, 2005; Richelle and Lejeune, 1980).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work on brain timing mechanisms.

claims.claim: In decision-making, a temporal delay is associated with the certainty of sensory information.
claims.source: In decision-making, animals choose one from multiple behavioral options based on environmental sensory information, where a temporal delay is associated with the certainty of sensory information.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about decision-making.

claims.claim: The cellular and molecular bases of simple decision-making have been studied in invertebrate animals because of the simplicity and accessibility of their nervous systems.
claims.source: The cellular and molecular bases of simple decision-making have been studied in invertebrate animals because of the simplicity and accessibility of their nervous systems (Kristan, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work on invertebrate decision-making.

results.result: C. elegans exhibits efficient directional choice during 2-nonanone avoidance, with 78.4% of runs initiated away from the odor source and 83.5% of ongoing runs directed away. This efficiency exceeds salt-taxis (59.3%) and is comparable to Drosophila larvae odor-taxis (73.9%). Animals choose appropriate directions through multiple exploratory migrations during pirouettes, which contain significantly more turns (5.2) than salt-taxis pirouettes (2.2).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide converging behavioral evidence from multi-worm tracking experiments (n=100 animals) with appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney, p<0.001). The directional choice percentages are well-documented in Figure 1B, and comparisons to salt-taxis and Drosophila are supported by both new data and appropriate citations. The 'pivot-and-go' strategy is clearly distinguished from random walk.

results.result: Behavioral states (pirouettes vs. runs) correlate with temporal changes in odor concentration (dCworm/dt). During pirouettes, dCworm/dt is mostly positive (animals stationary while odor increases), while during runs dCworm/dt is mostly negative (animals migrate down gradient). The relationship between responsiveness and dCworm/dt differs significantly between states, indicating they are physiologically distinct.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 are supported by quantitative odor gradient measurements (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and behavioral tracking data. The correlation analysis in Figure 2D demonstrates distinct responsiveness patterns. The odor gradient measurement methodology is rigorous with gas chromatography calibration and multiple replicates (7-9 per condition).

results.result: Two distinct sensory pathways regulate odor avoidance behavior opposingly: AWB neurons respond to odor decreases by gradually activating over 90s and suppressing turns when optogenetically activated, while ASH neurons respond to odor increases and promote turns when active. Optogenetic inactivation of ASH during odor increases significantly suppresses turning rate increases.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C17 are supported by calcium imaging data (Figure 3C, 3E) and optogenetic manipulation experiments (Figure 3D, 3F) using the OSB2 system. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.01 for AWB ChR2, p<0.05 for ASH Arch). The opposing regulation model is a reasonable inference from the combined data, though the neural circuit mechanisms downstream remain incompletely characterized.

results.result: ASH neurons compute time-differential responses to odor concentration increases. Responses peak rapidly after odor-up phase onset and can be approximated by dC/dt. This enables rapid, reflex-like behavioral responses to unfavorable odor changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C18 and C39 are supported by calcium imaging data across multiple dC/dt rates (Figure 4A) with mathematical modeling (Table 1). The time-differential model fits the data reasonably well, though the authors acknowledge some aspects (e.g., decay kinetics) are not perfectly captured. The rapid behavioral response correlation is demonstrated by turning rate exceeding 99% prediction intervals.

results.result: AWB neurons compute time-integral responses to odor concentration decreases via a leaky integrator mechanism. Calcium accumulation is gradual with rate-dependent delays (estimated basal [Ca2+]i ~60-90 nM), correlating with behavioral transitions from high- to low-turning states. The timing of behavioral transitions depends on dC/dt rate, with faster decreases causing shorter delays. This temporal integration represents 'evidence accumulation' for decision-making.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C21, C37-C38, C40 are supported by calcium imaging across multiple dC/dt rates (Figure 4B), mathematical modeling with leaky integrator equations (Tables 2-3), and calcium concentration estimation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The correlation between AWB activity and behavioral transitions is demonstrated with 99% prediction intervals. The BIC analysis (Table 3) shows leaky integrator fits better than simple differentiation. The 'evidence accumulation' interpretation is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Computer simulations demonstrate that temporal integration of dC/dt produces appropriate directional choice similar to real animals, while simple differentiation significantly worsens directional choice (p<0.001, Mardia-Watson-Wheeler test).
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C24 are supported by computational modeling (Figure 5) with appropriate statistical comparison. The simulation parameters are based on measured behavioral statistics. However, the model is simplified (e.g., sinusoidal head movement is less complex than reality), and the authors acknowledge this limitation. The result supports the functional importance of temporal integration but doesn't prove it's the only mechanism.

results.result: Temporal integration in AWB neurons occurs within the neuron itself and does not require recurrent synaptic circuits, as demonstrated by preserved AWB responses in unc-13 and unc-31 mutants that abolish synaptic transmission.
results.evaluation: Claim C25 is supported by calcium imaging in unc-13 and unc-31 mutants (Figure 6A, Table 2) showing responses fitted by the same leaky integrator equations as wild-type. This is a critical mechanistic finding distinguishing single-cell from circuit-based integration. The genetic approach is appropriate, though the authors note these mutations affect 'most, if not all' neurons, leaving some uncertainty about completeness.

results.result: ODR-3 Gα protein plays a time-differential role in AWB sensory signaling. In odr-3 mutants, the time-differential property is degraded (Δt >60s vs 1s in wild-type) while time-integral property is preserved. ODR-3 is homologous to inhibitory Gαi proteins and may function in an inhibitory feed-forward loop to compute time-differentials.
results.evaluation: Claims C26 and C41 are supported by calcium imaging in two odr-3 alleles (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) with mathematical modeling showing better fits with long Δt (Table 2, Table 4). The inhibitory feed-forward loop model is speculative but reasonable given ODR-3's homology to Gαi (cited to Bargmann 2006 and Alon 2007). The finding that time-integral property is preserved while time-differential is lost is particularly compelling.

results.result: Calcium accumulation in AWB neurons depends primarily on influx through EGL-19 L-type VGCCs. The egl-19 reduction-of-function mutation and EGL-19 antagonist Nemadipine-A significantly affect AWB responses, while mutations in unc-2 (N-type), itr-1 (IP3R), or unc-68 (RyR) do not.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 are supported by genetic and pharmacological experiments (Figure 7A, 7C). The selective requirement for EGL-19 is demonstrated by multiple approaches. Statistical significance is shown (p<0.001, Kruskal-Wallis with Steel-Dwass). However, the claim that calcium accumulation 'mostly depends' on EGL-19 is an inference from loss-of-function data; quantitative contribution is not determined.

results.result: ASH response consists of fast and slow components. EGL-19 suppression affects the later phase but not the initial response. The fast component is not mediated by typical VGCCs (unc-2, cca-1 mutations have no effect) but may involve unidentified calcium channels. Both components are amplified by CICR via ITR-1 and UNC-68, which partially affect magnitude but not temporal pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 are supported by genetic and pharmacological experiments (Figure 7B, 7C, 7D). The two-component model is supported by mathematical reconstruction (Figure 7D). However, the 'unidentified calcium channels' for the fast component remain speculative—the negative results with unc-2 and cca-1 don't prove other channels are involved. The CICR amplification is well-supported by multiple approaches (itr-1, unc-68 mutations and dantrolene).

results.result: C. elegans olfactory behavior comprises discrete behavioral choice based on dC/dt (pirouette vs. run states), analogous to evidence accumulation in mammalian perceptual decision-making. Both involve temporal integration of sensory information for decision-making.
results.evaluation: Claims C36 and C43 synthesize the behavioral and neural findings into a decision-making framework. The discrete state transitions are well-documented (C9-C10, Figure 2D). The analogy to mammalian decision-making is supported by appropriate citations (Gold and Shadlen 2007, Schall 2001) and is conceptually reasonable given the temporal integration mechanism. However, this remains an interpretive framework rather than direct evidence of homology.

results.result: L-type VGCCs are activated continuously during depolarization, unlike N/P/Q-type or T-type VGCCs.
results.evaluation: Claim C42 is supported by citation to established knowledge (Hille 2001). This is accurate general knowledge about VGCC biophysics that supports the authors' model for how EGL-19 mediates gradual calcium accumulation.

results.result: In higher animals, temporally integrating neural activity for decision-making and working memory is generally considered to be mediated by recurrent neural circuits, though intracellular mechanisms (NMDA receptors, CAN channels, VGCCs) have been proposed theoretically but not demonstrated experimentally prior to this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45, C52-C53 accurately represent the state of the field based on appropriate citations (Gold and Shadlen 2007, Wang 2008, Curtis and Lee 2010, Major and Tank 2004). This contextualizes the novelty of the authors' finding of single-cell temporal integration.

results.result: Background knowledge and prior work establishing: C. elegans odor avoidance behavior and navigation strategies; decision-making mechanisms in mammals and invertebrates; AWB and ASH neuron functions; calcium signaling mechanisms; GCaMP3 properties; genetic tools (unc-13, unc-31, odr-3, calcium channel genes); and general neuroscience principles.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C94 represent background knowledge, prior work, and established facts that are appropriately cited and accurately represented. These provide essential context for interpreting the current findings. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the cited literature.
